clue.text: Repeatedly stretch point?

parts.note: a stretch is a spell in prison
and the answer names in full the relation of one following the other

explanation.surface: Bending a rule further than you should, over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the clue says 'after': the phrase supplies it, and the question mark is the setter owning up. Stretch and point are both time, one of them long and one of them instant.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something time after time is doing it repeatedly; the phrase is the idiom for endless recurrence.

clue.text: When empty, rule 1 is to fill glasses for salutations

indicators.note: a word emptied has had its insides taken out, leaving the letters at either end

parts.note: RULE with its middle emptied keeps R…E

indicators.note: filling something means going inside it, so this letter is dropped into the middle

parts.note: specs are glasses
the answer at 1 down is TIME, and t is the abbreviation for it

explanation.surface: The first rule of hosting: keep everyone's glass topped up for the toasts.
explanation.walkthrough: It is 'rule' that gets emptied, not 'when' — the comma is placed to make you try the wrong word. The number is a cross-reference to 1 down, which supplies a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To pay your respects is to send salutations; both words are the plural noun for a formal greeting.

clue.text: Group left in trouble in retirement

indicators.note: 'in' puts the piece before it inside the piece after it
something in retirement has gone back, and letters going back are written in reverse

parts.note: the rub is the trouble — 'there's the rub'
l = left

explanation.surface: Someone abandoned in difficulty the moment their working life ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Group' is pointing at Britpop rather than at any collection of things — the band took their name from a verb meaning to smudge. Two 'in's do different jobs, one enclosing and one turning round.
explanation.definitionFit: Blur are a British band, and a band is a group — definition by example, with the capital hidden by the clue's first word.

clue.text: News account breaking down summit

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so these letters go in the middle

parts.note: pile is the soft raised surface of a carpet or velvet, as down is the soft covering on a bird
n = new, and the s makes it plural: two of them
a/c = account

explanation.surface: A news report of a summit meeting collapsing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'News' is the trick: not information at all, but N for new made plural. The summit is a mountain top, not the conference the surface has convened.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinnacle is the topmost point of anything — the summit of a mountain, or of a career.

clue.text: Folly of international firm returning self-assembly boxes

indicators.note: boxes means the do-it-yourself letters enclose the turned-round firm

parts.note: DIY, do-it-yourself, covers putting things together yourself

indicators.note: returning means the firm's letters come back the other way

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A dig at a global furniture company whose flat-pack boxes keep coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns CO into OC, and 'boxes' puts OC inside DIY. The surface hints at a Swedish flat-pack retailer, but no name is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiocy is foolish behaviour, and folly likewise means a lack of good sense.

clue.text: Thrash a legal case for trial out — it's iron-clad

indicators.note: it's points to the whole rearranged result as the thing wrapped by the metal
iron-clad means the iron symbol wraps around the rest

parts.note: FE is the chemical symbol for iron

indicators.note: out here means wrong or in disarray, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside, so only its first and last letters are kept

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lawyer bragging that a court case is watertight and will thrash the opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case for' trial gives TL; 'out' rearranges A, LEGAL and TL; 'clad' puts all that inside FE, so 'iron-clad' is split across two jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: To flagellate is to whip or flog someone, a literal sense of thrashing.

clue.text: If not, French articles succeeded

parts.note: un is the French for 'a'
les is the French 'the' in front of a plural
s = succeeded

explanation.surface: Otherwise, it was the pieces written in French that did well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' is plural for a reason: the wordplay wants two of them, and French keeps a whole drawerful. The grammar-book words are worth collecting — UN, UNE, LE, LA, LES.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Unless it rains' and 'if it does not rain' set the same condition, so the two open a clause the same way.

clue.text: Model bounced online to experience ecstasy

indicators.note: to model something is to mould it, and letters moulded afresh come out in another order

parts.note: anagram fodder, thirteen letters

explanation.surface: A model thrown off the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' looks like the noun the surface needs and is really a verb: to model is to shape. Ecstasy here is the feeling rather than the pill, which is why the answer is a state of mind.
explanation.definitionFit: To be on cloud nine is to be blissfully happy — the idiom for experiencing ecstasy.

clue.text: Regularly birdie and occasionally eagle — perfect

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at a fixed interval, so the letters are taken at a fixed interval too
occasionally means now and then rather than throughout, so only some of the letters are used

parts.note: every second letter of b-I-r-D-i-E
every second letter of e-A-g-L-e

explanation.surface: A golfer's card: birdies most rounds, an eagle now and again.
explanation.walkthrough: Two extractions of the same kind, from a pair of words that sit together naturally: in golf a birdie is one under par and an eagle two. Both runs start at the second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An ideal arrangement is a perfect one; the adjective slots in wherever 'perfect' would.

clue.text: Laziness in Céline Dion cast — one is dropped

indicators.note: cast means thrown or moulded afresh, so the letters are reshaped
is dropped means the letter for one is taken out of the pool

parts.note: the singer's name, taken as the pool of letters
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A grumble that the cast of a Céline Dion show has lost a member through idleness.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove I ('one is dropped') from CELINE DION and 'cast' the rest into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: Indolence is a habitual avoidance of effort, which is exactly what laziness means.

clue.text: Language from mum, say, when A&E switch over tablets at the outset

indicators.note: at the outset puts the tablets at the very start

parts.note: Es are ecstasy tablets, slang for the pills

indicators.note: when A and E change places in the parent word, the letters A, R, E become E, R, A

parts.note: a mum is an example of a parent
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A hospital scene: a mother in casualty, staff swapping her medication.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A&E switch' swaps the A and E in PARENT to give PERANT; 'at the outset' puts ES first, and O ends it. A&E is the British hospital accident and emergency department.
explanation.definitionFit: Esperanto is the constructed international tongue devised by Zamenhof in 1887, so it is a language.

clue.text: Eco-friendly facts about drilling

indicators.note: a drill bores into the middle of something, and that is where these letters go

parts.note: gen is British slang for information — the facts
re = about, as at the head of a memo

explanation.surface: Environmentally sound information about drilling for oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is the letters rather than the instruction, which is the neat swap here: the instruction is 'drilling'. Gen, for information, comes out of wartime services slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Green is the everyday word for anything eco-friendly — green energy, green policies.

clue.text: Antique sabre — every now and then American cuts with it

indicators.note: now and then is not every time, so the letters are taken at intervals

parts.note: every second letter of s-A-b-R-e

indicators.note: to cut into something is to open it up and get inside

parts.note: someone chic is with it — stylish
a = American

explanation.surface: An old sword, and the American who now and then slices with it.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash lets 'sabre' look like part of the definition while it is working for the wordplay. 'With it' as slang for fashionable dates from the 1960s, which is half the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaic and antique both describe something belonging to an age long gone, and both are adjectives.

clue.text: See 1
Better speak with a married priest first

indicators.note: what comes first stands at the head of the answer, ahead of everything else

parts.note: used literally
m = married, as on a form
Eli is the priest who brought up Samuel in the Old Testament
to orate is to speak formally

explanation.surface: Advice to have a word with the married priest before anyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' is the verb, to improve, not the comparative the surface is reaching for. Eli, priest at Shiloh, is one of the handful of Bible names every setter keeps to hand.
explanation.definitionFit: To ameliorate a situation is to better it; the definition is the same transitive verb as the answer.

clue.text: Spooner's drunk talk — it could confirm pregnancy

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, which signals that swap here

parts.note: a soak is a heavy drinker, a drunk
yak is informal for chatter or talk

explanation.surface: A boozer rambling on about whether someone might be expecting.
explanation.walkthrough: SOAK YAK, said with the first sounds swapped, comes out as YOKE SACK; that is spelt YOLK SAC (the yolk's L is silent). A yolk sac seen on an early ultrasound scan confirms a pregnancy.
explanation.definitionFit: The yolk sac is the first structure visible on an early scan, and its presence is a medical sign that a pregnancy is under way.

clue.text: See 8
Liking a street in middle of Cheltenham

indicators.note: 'in' drops what comes before it inside what comes after

parts.note: the two central letters of chelTEnham
st = street in an address

indicators.note: only the letters at the centre of the word are wanted, and the rest are discarded

parts.note: used literally

explanation.surface: A fondness for one particular road in the centre of Cheltenham.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheltenham, a spa town in Gloucestershire, is here only for its middle — ten letters, so the centre comes out as a tidy pair rather than a single one.
explanation.definitionFit: A taste for something is a liking for it: 'she has a taste for opera' takes either noun.

clue.text: Bird's thigh bone discovered

indicators.note: dis-covered: with its cover removed, the word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: the femur is the thigh bone

explanation.surface: An archaeological find: a bird's thigh bone unearthed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discovered' reads as found, but here it means uncovered, the outer letters of FEMUR stripped away.
explanation.definitionFit: The emu is a large flightless Australian bird, related to the ostrich.

clue.text: Shout with gun going off — it's not called for

indicators.note: a gun going off explodes, and an explosion scatters whatever it touches

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A shout and a gun going off, neither of them wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: Look at the fodder: 'shout' and 'gun' are a shotgun with one letter adrift, which is how the surface stays so natural while carrying an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Advice that is unsought was never asked for, which is exactly what 'not called for' says of it.

clue.text: Trouble with Daily Telegraph's leaders stopping supplement

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its head, the one out in front

parts.note: ado is fuss or trouble — much ado about nothing

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so these letters are pushed into the middle

parts.note: the initials of the British national newspaper

explanation.surface: The Daily Telegraph's bosses blocking a supplement, to everyone's annoyance.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the clue mean two things: 'leaders' is senior management on the surface and initial letters underneath, while 'supplement' is a magazine insert on the surface and a verb in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To supplement a total is to add to it, and both are the transitive verb for topping something up.

clue.text: Remains when Oscar leaves largest city in Michigan, America

indicators.note: leaves means the letter departs from the city's name

parts.note: Detroit is the biggest city in the US state of Michigan
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A story of urban decline: what is left behind when someone departs the Motor City.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' takes O out of DETROIT, leaving DETRIT, and US follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Detritus is debris or waste left behind, the leftover remains of something broken down.

clue.text: Cancel theatre's Cinderella following cuts

indicators.note: cuts trim away the ends, and what is left standing after them is the run of letters you want

parts.note: the letters run on from the middle of the first word into the second, straight across the apostrophe and the space

explanation.surface: A theatre dropping its pantomime after the funding is cut.
explanation.walkthrough: Cinderella is the staple British pantomime, which is why a theatre would have one to lose in the first place. Punctuation counts for nothing in a hidden run: theat-RE’S CIND-erella.
explanation.definitionFit: To rescind an order is to cancel it; both are the verb for revoking something already issued.

clue.text: Enough to support son, 17

definitions.note: The definition is a cross-reference: 17 is the entry at 17 across, whose answer TASTE is the word being defined.

indicators.note: in a down entry whatever does the supporting has to sit underneath the thing it is holding up

parts.note: s = son
ample means enough and a bit over

explanation.surface: Money enough to keep a son going.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma does the damage: 'son, 17' looks like a boy and his age, and is really son plus a pointer to another entry. Down clues stack, so the supporting piece goes below.
explanation.definitionFit: To sample a dish is to taste it, which is the word waiting at 17 across.

clue.text: Perhaps Deborah Meaden's doctor detailed extreme suffering

indicators.note: de-tailed: with its tail cut off, the word loses its last letter

parts.note: agony is extreme pain or suffering

explanation.surface: A reality-TV investor's medical history: a doctor describing her pain in depth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' reads as thorough, but means the tail of AGONY comes off. Deborah Meaden is an investor on the BBC show Dragons' Den, whose panellists are called dragons.
explanation.definitionFit: On the British TV programme Dragons' Den, the wealthy investors judging pitches are known as dragons, and Meaden is one.

clue.text: Tense during drama initially directed like some soaps?

indicators.note: initially means at the very start, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: a scene is a unit of drama

indicators.note: whatever happens during something happens inside it, between its start and its end

parts.note: t = tense in grammar
the opening letter of directed

explanation.surface: A tense passage of drama, directed the way soap operas are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soaps' are the bars in the bathroom, not the serials the rest of the surface is busy filming — drama, scene and direction are all there to keep you in the studio.
explanation.definitionFit: Scented soap is soap that has been perfumed, and the question mark concedes that only some of it is.

clue.text: Powerless monkey — one seen in a circus?

indicators.note: powerless means without power, and power is what the letter p stands for

parts.note: to monkey with something is to tamper with it

explanation.surface: A feeble monkey, of the sort you might see under the big top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Monkey' is the verb, not the animal the circus invites you to picture: to monkey with something is to interfere with it. The definition has a different beast in mind altogether.
explanation.definitionFit: The tamer is the circus performer who works the lions, so 'one seen in a circus' names a person rather than an act.

clue.text: See 1
Modern day translation of Latin essentially Your Worship

parts.note: AD, anno domini, is how the modern era is dated

indicators.note: a translation gives you the same thing in a different arrangement of words, and here the letters come out rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder

indicators.note: the essence of a word is what sits at its heart, so only the middle letters are used

parts.note: the middle letters of yOUr

explanation.surface: A present-day rendering of some Latin, addressed to Your Worship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Your Worship' is how a mayor or a magistrate is addressed in Britain, which is what puts the surface in a council chamber. Only the second word of it is the definition; the first gives up its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Adulation is praise poured on somebody past all proportion — worship of a person rather than a god.

clue.text: Distributing small — not large — handouts

indicators.note: distributing means spreading out, so the letters are scattered into a new order
not tells us the large letter is missing from the pool

parts.note: taken as written, as the pool of letters
L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A charity giving out small gifts rather than large ones.
explanation.walkthrough: Take L ('not large') out of SMALL and rearrange the rest ('Distributing').
explanation.definitionFit: Alms are money or food given to the poor, charitable gifts handed out to those in need.

clue.text: See 8
Kind to insect assuming one might be found under a pillow?

definitions.text: one might be found under a pillow?
definitions.note: The definition describes the answer rather than standing in for it: what is named is the thing a child leaves there for the fairy to collect.

indicators.note: to assume something is to take it on, and here the word takes these letters on board inside itself

parts.note: a moth is an insect
people of your ilk are people of your kind
used literally

explanation.surface: Sparing an insect you suspect is under your pillow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind' is the noun, ilk, not the adjective the surface is being — and the insect swallows it whole along with the little word after it. The definition is pointing at the fairy who leaves a coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A child's first set of teeth are the ones that fall out and get left under the pillow in exchange for a coin.

clue.text: Keen — having second go after wasting first

parts.note: a mo is a moment — half a mo
a go is a TURN, which loses the letter at its front

explanation.surface: Eager for another turn, having squandered the first one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' is the verb here — to keen is to wail aloud over the dead, an Irish word long since naturalised — not the adjective the surface wants. 'Mo' is the British half a mo.
explanation.definitionFit: To keen is to lament the dead out loud, so it names the act of grieving that the answer covers more broadly.
